question: Software Factories
content: Guillermo Rauch describes a fundamental shift in how engineers are evaluated. The old framing was the '10x engineer' — someone who produces ten times the output of an average engineer. The new framing moves beyond individual multipliers to something more systemic.
description: You are a CTO evaluating your engineering team's performance now that AI handles most implementation work. A board member asks how you measure whether an engineer is 'good enough' in the AI age. Using Guillermo Rauch's framework, what should you look for?
options: How many pull requests they close per week using AI coding assistance tools
Whether they are producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z
How many tokens they consume from the AI model on a daily basis at work
How quickly they can debug production issues and incidents using AI tools
answer: Whether they are producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z
explanation: Guillermo Rauch says the shift is from 'you are a 10x engineer' to judging whether 'you are producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z.' It's not about individual output; it's about creating the systems that compound output.

question: The 1000x Engineer
content: Naval reflects on the long-running controversy around the concept of 10x engineers — developers who produce vastly more value than their peers. He cites famous examples to make his point and then explains what has changed in the AI era.
description: A founder on your team argues that '10x engineers don't really exist' and that everyone is roughly equally productive. You recall Naval's perspective on this debate. What does Naval say is the actual productivity spread, and why is it now less controversial?
options: 10x engineers exist, but the spread is only noticeable in large companies
Productivity differences are at most 2x because tools tend to equalize most skill gaps
It's not even 10x — it's 100x or 1000x, and AI leverage now makes it obvious
The concept of 10x engineers existed before cloud computing but does not apply in the AI era
answer: It's not even 10x — it's 100x or 1000x, and AI leverage now makes it obvious
explanation: Naval says he used to get flamed for claiming 10x engineers exist, citing Satoshi and John Carmack as examples of 1000x programmers. AI leverage now makes extreme productivity differences less controversial and more visible.

question: The New Lines of Code
content: As companies adopt AI coding tools, managers look for new metrics to measure productivity. Token consumption and model usage are common candidates. Blake Scholl offers a historical analogy for why this is misguided.
description: Your VP of Engineering proposes tracking AI token spend per developer as a key productivity metric, arguing that more tokens means more done. What would Blake Scholl say about token consumption as a measure of output?
options: Token consumption is the most accurate measure of developer AI productivity available today
Token consumption is like the old measuring of lines of code — a vanity metric
Token consumption should be minimized because it directly drives up operational cloud costs
High token consumption always indicates a developer is struggling with how to prompt the AI effectively
answer: Token consumption is like the old measuring of lines of code — a vanity metric
explanation: Blake Scholl directly says measuring by token consumption is 'like the old measuring of lines of code' — a proxy that doesn't capture true output, quality, or value.

question: The Competence Mirror
content: Max Hodak observes that team members experience AI coding tools very differently depending on their skill level. This creates a puzzle for managers: the same tool gets radically different reviews from different engineers.
description: A junior engineer on your team says Claude isn't that helpful — it gives vague answers and wastes time. A senior engineer insists Claude is the most powerful tool they've ever used. According to Max Hodak, what explains this discrepancy?
options: The senior engineer pays for and has access to a more capable premium AI model subscription than the junior developer
AI models reflect back the competence of the user — they are as good as you are in the domain
The junior engineer is likely using the wrong programming language and framework for writing their AI queries and prompts
The AI model has stale and outdated training data and only works well with older deprecated frameworks and library versions
answer: AI models reflect back the competence of the user — they are as good as you are in the domain
explanation: Max Hodak explains: 'Claude or ChatGPT is basically as good as you are in a domain. If you're a really capable developer, these things are really powerful. If you're a junior developer, you'll find it to be more of a junior developer.'

question: The New Support Skill
content: Guillermo Rauch describes a new kind of help he now provides to colleagues who struggle with AI tools. The bottleneck is no longer access to the model — it's knowing how to communicate with it effectively.
description: A teammate comes to you frustrated because they spent an hour prompting the AI model and got unusable results. They ask for your help. According to Guillermo Rauch, what form should your help take in the age of AI?
options: Take over and write the entire implementation yourself to save them time and frustration
Recommend that they switch to a different AI model that is more reliable for this task
Tell them what to prompt the model with — the quality of reprompting is critical
Suggest they completely abandon the AI approach and write all the code manually instead
answer: Tell them what to prompt the model with — the quality of reprompting is critical
explanation: Guillermo Rauch says: 'There's a new kind of support I give now — you come to me, you didn't get good output out of the model, and I tell you what to prompt the model with. The quality of the reprompting is extremely important.'

question: Waste Tokens, Save Time
content: Naval describes his deliberately low-effort approach to using AI models. Instead of optimizing prompts and carefully crafting queries, he takes a completely different philosophy that prioritizes time over token cost.
description: You find yourself spending 15 minutes carefully crafting the perfect prompt to minimize token usage and API costs. Naval would say your focus is misplaced. What does he recommend instead?
options: Spend a lot of time studying advanced prompt engineering techniques and frameworks in order to maximize your token efficiency at work
Waste tokens to save time — tokens are way cheaper than a human and you can always buy more
Build a local caching layer for common API responses to reduce expensive model calls and costs
Switch to using only open-source AI models that have zero per-token inference cost to save money
answer: Waste tokens to save time — tokens are way cheaper than a human and you can always buy more
explanation: Naval says: 'I just assumed the model is going to get better faster than I would figure out how to use it... Just waste tokens to save time. No matter how expensive these models might seem, they're still way cheaper than a human.'

question: The Principal Engineer Model
content: Guillermo Rauch describes a recent inflection point in how AI models interact with developers. The models no longer just execute — they push back, suggest alternatives, and evaluate trade-offs, which changes the human-AI dynamic entirely.
description: You notice that your AI coding assistant no longer just implements what you ask. Instead, it frequently responds with 'Here's what I'd recommend, but there are trade-offs to consider...' and lists alternatives. How does Guillermo Rauch characterize this shift?
options: The model is hallucinating more than usual and needs stricter constraints
The model has graduated from a junior engineer to a principal engineer level
This is a temporary glitch from a bad model update that will be patched
The model is trying to avoid work by overcomplicating simple requests
answer: The model has graduated from a junior engineer to a principal engineer level
explanation: Guillermo Rauch observes: 'The models at some point graduated. They used to be junior engineers. Now they're principal engineers, because they come back to you with a set of trade-offs and plans before starting.'

question: You Don't Get Stuck Anymore
content: Max Hodak describes the most profound change AI has brought to building software. Every developer knows the frustration of hitting a wall for hours or days on a seemingly small problem. AI agents fundamentally change this dynamic.
description: You remember spending three days debugging a race condition in your first job — reading docs, searching Stack Overflow, trying random permutations. Max Hodak argues this painful experience is now optional. What changed?
options: Programming languages have evolved to become simpler and eliminated race conditions and deadlocks entirely
Modern debuggers now have built-in AI that automatically detects and fixes all concurrency related bugs
With agents, you just don't get stuck anymore — they can quickly find the right way to do things
AI generated error messages have become so incredibly descriptive that no manual debugging or searching through documentation is ever needed
answer: With agents, you just don't get stuck anymore — they can quickly find the right way to do things
explanation: Max Hodak says: 'It used to be you could build a lot, a lot would go straightforward, but then you'd hit some random thing and you could spend an indefinite period of time debugging some narrow thing. Now, with agents, you just don't get stuck anymore.'

question: Vibe Coding Through People
content: Guillermo Rauch and Naval discuss a parallel between how engineering leaders have always operated and how people now interact with AI agents. The description of working through agents sounds familiar to anyone who has led teams.
description: Someone watches you iterating with an AI agent — describing what you want, reviewing the output, giving feedback in natural language — and calls it 'vibe coding.' Naval and Guillermo recognize this pattern from something else. What?
options: It mirrors how junior developers learn from senior code reviews
Engineering leaders have always been vibe coding through people on Slack
It's the same as pair programming but with a faster partner
It resembles how founders pitch to venture capitalists for feedback
answer: Engineering leaders have always been vibe coding through people on Slack
explanation: Guillermo Rauch and Naval point out that engineering leaders have described what they do as 'vibe coding through people on Slack' — telling people what to do, reviewing output, iterating. The only change is the agent replaces the human executor.

question: Is Pure Software Dead?
content: Naval poses a provocative question about the future of software as a business. When AI models can write code as easily as humans speak English, the traditional moats of software engineering may dissolve. This forces a rethinking of what is actually valuable.
description: A founder pitches you a pure SaaS product whose only competitive advantage is the codebase. Naval would likely question this pitch. What foundational question is Naval asking about the software industry that applies here?
options: When will AI replace all software engineers and make coding skills completely obsolete forever?
Is pure software dead — is classic software engineering becoming an obsolete thing?
Should all startups pivot to selling AI models instead of building software products?
Will the widespread adoption of open-source eventually make commercial software illegal to sell?
answer: Is pure software dead — is classic software engineering becoming an obsolete thing?
explanation: Naval asks: 'Is pure software dead? Is pure software engineering an obsolete thing? It's like saying speaking English — the models now speak English.' He suggests hardware moats and model-building may be the new durable advantages.
